prompt: linkbox's container started with plain `docker run`. Which restriction did `docker inspect` show was in place?

choices.text: A read-only root filesystem
choices.why: `read-only=false`: the root was writable.

choices.text: A memory limit of 256 MB
choices.why: `memory=0` means no limit at all.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: Right: no capability dropped, no security option, no limit. Only the seccomp filter, which `inspect` does not list here, was on.

choices.text: Every capability dropped
choices.why: `cap-drop=[]`: nothing was dropped.

prompt: In the default container, `CapEff` was 0 and `CapBnd` was `00000000a80425fb`. What does that pair mean?

choices.text: None held now; fourteen within reach
choices.why: Right. The bounding set is the ceiling for a root process or a setuid file.

choices.text: The process holds fourteen capabilities and uses none
choices.why: Effective is what it holds for use; zero effective means it holds none to use.

choices.text: Docker failed to drop the capabilities it was asked to drop
choices.why: Nobody asked; this was a plain `docker run`.

choices.text: The seccomp filter is blocking fourteen calls
choices.why: Seccomp is the `Seccomp` line; the capability lines are a different mechanism.

prompt: As user 65532 the process could not change `/app/app.py`; started with `--user 0`, it could. What does that say about `USER` in a Dockerfile?

choices.text: A default, replaced by whoever starts it
choices.why: Right, which is why the later controls do not depend on the user.

choices.text: It is enforced by the kernel for the life of the image
choices.why: The kernel enforces whatever user the process actually runs as, and that is chosen at start.

choices.text: It only matters at build time, for `RUN` lines
choices.why: It sets the user the container starts as, too: 65532 here unless overridden.

choices.text: It makes the files of `/app` read-only
choices.why: Ownership made them unwritable for 65532; root could still write them.

prompt: The kernel's summary of a process, which the lesson read for its user, capabilities and seccomp state, is the file `/proc/<pid>/___`
Run read-only with no other change, linkbox's container exits. What does the log say it needed?

choices.text: A writable `/data` for the SQLite file
choices.why: That is the second failure, once gunicorn starts; the first comes earlier.

choices.text: A usable temporary directory
choices.why: Right: `No usable temporary directory found`, raised by `tempfile` for gunicorn's worker heartbeat file.

choices.text: Permission to bind port 8000
choices.why: Binding a port above 1024 needs no capability and no file.

choices.text: A shell to run its start script
choices.why: There is no start script and no shell; gunicorn starts directly.

prompt: With `--tmpfs /tmp` added, the container stays up and the first POST answers 500. Why is this failure the more dangerous of the two?

choices.text: It corrupts the database
choices.why: Nothing was written; SQLite could not even open the file.

choices.text: It looks healthy until somebody uses it
choices.why: Right. A check that only looks at whether the container started passes it.

choices.text: It leaks the token in the error page
choices.why: The 500 carried no token; the error went to the log.

choices.text: It restarts in a loop and fills the disk
choices.why: The container stayed up; nothing restarted.

prompt: `/tmp` is a `tmpfs` mounted `noexec`. What does that stop, and what does it not?

choices.text: It stops any code in `/tmp` from running, including Python files
choices.why: `python3 file.py` runs the interpreter, which lives elsewhere; the file is only read.

choices.text: It stops writes to `/tmp` but not reads
choices.why: `/tmp` is mounted `rw`; writing is the reason it exists.

choices.text: Executing a file there as a program; an interpreter reading it still works
choices.why: Right, which is why the lesson does not stop at the filesystem.

choices.text: It stops nothing in a container with a read-only root
choices.why: The root is read-only; `/tmp` is a separate, writable mount with its own options.

prompt: Match each path in the read-only linkbox container with how it is mounted.
right_distractors: a named volume shared with the host

prompt: Root in a container started with `--cap-drop ALL` tries `os.chown('/data', 0, 0)`. What happens, and why?

choices.text: It works: root can always change owners
choices.why: Changing an owner needs `CAP_CHOWN`, and the bounding set is empty.

choices.text: `Operation not permitted`: no `CAP_CHOWN`
choices.why: Right. Same command, same user 0; only the capability differs.

choices.text: `Read-only file system`: `/data` is part of the image
choices.why: That run had no `--read-only`; the refusal came from the missing capability.

choices.text: The container refuses to start as root
choices.why: Docker starts it as root without complaint; Kubernetes' `runAsNonRoot` is what refuses user 0.

prompt: The distroless image has no setuid file under `/usr`. A colleague says `no-new-privileges` is therefore pointless for linkbox. What is the lesson's answer?

choices.text: It guards the next image
choices.why: Right: the next image is the one nobody checks for setuid files, and the flag costs nothing to a program that never needed new privileges.

choices.text: He is right; the flag only matters on images with a shell
choices.why: A setuid file needs no shell to be executed; any program can exec it.

choices.text: It also blocks system calls that seccomp lets through
choices.why: Seccomp filters calls; `no-new-privileges` is about privilege gained by executing a file.

choices.text: It drops the capabilities that `--cap-drop ALL` leaves
choices.why: `--cap-drop ALL` leaves none; the two flags do different things.

prompt: A server must listen on port 80. Following the lesson, how should its container be started?

choices.text: With the default capabilities, since it needs one of them
choices.why: That keeps thirteen it does not need within reach.

choices.text: `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE`
choices.why: Right: drop everything, add back the one, and justify it on review.

choices.text: As `--user 0`, because binding below 1024 needs root
choices.why: It needs one capability, not root; root brings all fourteen.

choices.text: With `--privileged`, for the port and nothing else
choices.why: `--privileged` grants every capability and device; it is the opposite of the lesson.

prompt: Which of these controls hold whatever user the process runs as? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `--read-only`
choices.why: Right: `--user 0` got `Read-only file system` too.

choices.text: `USER 65532` in the Dockerfile
choices.why: That one is the user, and `--user 0` replaces it.

choices.text: `--cap-drop ALL`
choices.why: Right: root without capabilities could not `chown`.

choices.text: `--security-opt no-new-privileges`
choices.why: Right: it holds for every process in the container and cannot be cleared.

choices.text: files owned by root in `/app`
choices.why: Ownership protects them from 65532 and not from root.

prompt: As root with default capabilities, `os.unshare(os.CLONE_NEWUSER)` failed; with `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` it worked. What refused it the first time?

choices.text: The missing `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` alone
choices.why: The capabilities were the same in both runs; only the filter changed.

choices.text: Docker's default seccomp profile
choices.why: Right: one run with the filter, one without, nothing else different.

choices.text: The read-only filesystem
choices.why: Neither run was read-only, and a namespace is not a file.

choices.text: AppArmor's docker-default profile
choices.why: The recording machine runs no AppArmor; the daemon listed only seccomp.

prompt: A process killed by the kernel's out-of-memory killer with `SIGKILL` (signal 9) leaves which exit status in `docker run`?
Why does the lesson set `--memory-swap` equal to `--memory`?

choices.text: So the limit is the limit, with no swap on top
choices.why: Right: equal values leave no room to swap beyond the memory limit.

choices.text: Because Docker refuses `--memory` without it
choices.why: Docker accepts `--memory` alone and adds swap of the same size by default on hosts with swap.

choices.text: To double the memory the container may use
choices.why: Equal values mean zero swap, not double.

choices.text: To make `OOMKilled` appear in `docker inspect`
choices.why: `OOMKilled` is recorded whenever the kernel kills for memory; swap does not decide that.

prompt: With `--pids-limit 32`, how many threads did `threads.py` start before one was refused?
linkbox used 39 MiB under a 256 MiB limit. A colleague proposes `--memory 40m` to make the limit tight. What does the lesson's reasoning predict?

choices.text: Better protection for the host at no cost
choices.why: The host was already protected by 256; 40 adds a cost and little protection.

choices.text: No effect: the limit only applies at start
choices.why: The limit applies for the container's whole life; that is how `hog` was killed.

choices.text: Kills on the first busy afternoon of traffic
choices.why: Right: a limit at today's idle use fails as soon as real traffic arrives.

choices.text: Docker rounds it up to 256 MiB anyway
choices.why: Docker applies the value it is given.

prompt: Why does the nightly dynamic scan now run linkbox read-only and without capabilities?

choices.text: To test what production runs
choices.why: Right, and a flag that breaks linkbox shows up there rather than at the first deployment.

choices.text: Because ZAP refuses to scan a privileged container
choices.why: ZAP only sends HTTP requests; it cannot see how its target was started.

choices.text: To find more warnings than lesson 4's scan
choices.why: The flags change the container, not what ZAP reports; the verdict stayed the same.

choices.text: So the scan finishes faster
choices.why: Speed did not change in any way that matters; that was never the reason.

prompt: Match each `docker run` flag of the staging script with the Kubernetes field lesson 10 uses for it.
Suppose a later version of linkbox writes cache files to `/var/cache/linkbox`. Nobody updates `ci/dast.sh`. Where is the problem first seen?

choices.text: In the push of the change, at the image stage
choices.why: The image stage scans packages; it never runs the application.

choices.text: In production, since staging ignores the filesystem
choices.why: Staging is read-only now, so the write fails there first.

choices.text: In the unit tests, which run read-only too
choices.why: The tests run in a virtual environment on the CI machine, not in the container.

choices.text: In the nightly scan of the read-only staging
choices.why: Right: the read-only staging container hits the write first, which is the point of making staging match production.

prompt: Put the method for running an unfamiliar image read-only in order.
items: exercise every route and job that writes
read the errors for the paths it failed to write
give each path a tmpfs or a volume
write the list into the script or manifest that starts it

prompt: Which statements about the container staging now runs are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: its bounding set is empty
its seccomp filter is off
choices.why: `Seccomp: 2`: the default filter stayed on.

choices.text: it can write to `/tmp` and `/data` and nowhere else
choices.why: Right: two tmpfs mounts on a read-only root.

choices.text: it has a 256 MiB memory limit
choices.why: Staging leaves the limits out; it lives for a minute.

choices.text: `NoNewPrivs` is 1 for every process in it
choices.why: Right: set at start and inherited by every child.
